transcript:
[00:00] Alex Carter (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to run a focused deep dive on Private VPC networking and how that impacts runtime performance — batching, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and what to expect with PrivateLink/NAT/subnet design.
[00:12] Sara Blake (Aurelius): Hi, thanks. We mostly want to understand latency tail behavior — our SLA is 100ms p95 for short chat completions and we'd like to know if private VPC adds jitter.
[00:25] Priya (SE): Great question. Short answer: you will see additional network hops with PrivateLink and NATs which can add a few ms, but the dominant tail is often model kv cache warm/cold and container spin-up. We'll walk the network path.
[00:40] Tom (SRE): Quick note — we're running in GCP us-central1 and have restrictive egress rules. We plan to use Private Google Access and also evaluate PrivateLink via interconnect.
[00:52] Miguel (Redwood SE): Okay. So typical Private deployment path: customer app in VPC -> NAT/egress -> PrivateLink endpoint <-> Redwood private runtime in a customer-managed VPC or peered VPC. You can also do VPC peering or AWS Transit if multi-account. Each hop adds small latency; PrivateLink keeps it inside the cloud fabric so it's usually lower jitter than public internet routes.
[01:15] Sara: Can you quantify? We need numbers to justify architecture to infra team.
[01:20] Priya: In our internal benchmarks we see median network add of ~1-3ms for PrivateLink inside same region, p95 around 5-10ms depending on NAT throughput and SNAT table exhaustion. If you cross region or go through additional transit, that grows. The runtime token generation itself is typically 30-80ms p50 for our optimized configs depending on model/sequence.
[01:40] Evan: You mentioned SNAT table exhaustion — we run many ephemeral workers, pool churn is high. What do you recommend?
[01:47] Miguel: For high-churn environments avoid heavy NAT translation: prefer private endpoints that use ENIs (PrivateLink) or assign EFA-like interfaces where supported. If NAT is unavoidable, ensure large port ranges and autoscaling for NAT gateways, and monitor ephemeral port exhaustion.
[02:00] Rina (Security): On the security side we need SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration for key wraps. Does Redwood support customer-managed KMS/HSM in Private?
[02:11] Alex: Yes, we support customer KMS for model keys and data encryption in Private deployments; HSM integrations are supported for enterprise contracts. Audit logs can be exported to your logging sink. We'll attach our security package.
[02:24] Sara: Back to runtime: how does KV cache behave across the network boundary? If the model KV cache lives on the runtime pods, will cold starts over PrivateLink suffer?
[02:36] Priya: The KV cache is local to the model worker — it's in-GPU memory or local host cache. Network only comes into play when you have a two-tier architecture (front-end route to centralized cache). For Redwood Private we keep KV on the same host or node pool. Cold starts are mainly due to model load/weight paging or cache miss across shards. Network adds only if you have cross-node cache fetches.
[02:58] Tom: So to guarantee low tail latency we should size pools to reduce cross-node KV misses?
[03:04] Priya: Exactly. We recommend pinning hot models to dedicated node pools and enabling local KV affinity. That reduces network fetches for KV and keeps p95 down.
[03:14] Evan: What about batching? We need throughput peaks for inference but cannot balloon latency for interactive requests.
[03:20] Miguel: Redwood runtime supports latency-aware batching and dynamic batching thresholds. For interactive routes we recommend small max batch sizes and short batching windows (e.g., 10-20ms). For high-throughput asynchronous jobs, larger batches give cost savings. You can set per-route SLOs: e.g., chat-fast route max batch 8, 15ms window; chat-batch route max batch 64, 100ms window.
[03:44] Sara: And quantization — we plan to use int8 quantized models to reduce cost. How does that affect latency/throughput?
[03:50] Priya: Quantization helps both throughput and memory; int8 can reduce per-token compute and increase batch concurrency. However there's a small CPU/GPU kernel overhead for dequant/requant and potential accuracy degradation. In practice we've seen median token latency reductions of 10-30% for mid-sized models when quantized, and throughput increases ~1.5-2x. We'll share model-specific perf profiles.
[04:10] Evan: Any caveats with Private VPC and quantized runtimes? Network-wise nothing special; the main concern is CPU/GPU kernel selection and pinned libraries. You may need exact CUDA/cuDNN versions in Private to match performance.
[04:22] Alex: Right — OS/kernel versions and TensorRT/LibTorch builds can change perf. For Private deployments we recommend standardizing node image versions; Redwood can provide AMI/container images pinned to validated stacks.
[04:34] Rina: On DNS — we have internal resolvers and strict split-horizon. How is service discovery handled for PrivateLink endpoints?
[04:42] Miguel: For AWS PrivateLink you create interface endpoints with ENIs in subnets. You can use private hosted zones and alias records to point to the endpoints. For split-horizon, ensure your resolver forwards to VPC resolver and that port 53 is open between your subnets and resolver. We also support explicit IPs in route tables if DNS can't be used.
[05:00] Tom: NAT egress costs are a concern. If we route through NAT for model telemetry or telemetry back to Redwood, what are our options to minimize cross-account egress?
[05:09] Priya: Options: use VPC peering or Transit Gateway to keep traffic inside cloud fabric, use PrivateLink to avoid NAT for control-plane traffic, and batch telemetry to reduce egress frequency. For telemetry we can also host an on-prem aggregator that forwards deltas. We'll show cost comparisons.
[05:24] Sara: Do you support multi-AZ deployments for resiliency? We need failover without large performance hits.
[05:30] Miguel: Yes, recommended: spread node pools across AZs but keep hot-model replicas in the primary AZ to avoid cross-AZ latency on KV fetch. For failover, keep standby replicas in other AZs with warmed weights; that way failover cost is a small increase in p95 but migration is quick.
[05:46] Evan: Can we get an example network diagram and Terraform for the PrivateLink flow?
[05:50] Alex: We'll attach diagrams and example IaC. Action: Priya will produce the perf test plan and Miguel will include a Terraform snippet.
[05:58] Rina: On compliance, any SOC2 gaps? We need to verify logging retention and key access controls.
[06:04] Alex: We'll send our SOC2 report and map controls to your checklist. KMS access is restricted and keys can be customer-managed; audit logs include token-level traces if you enable it.
[06:15] Tom: A smaller practical point — ephemeral port exhaustion. We have seen it bite when autoscaling spikes outbound connections. Does Redwood recommend connection pooling at app layer?
[06:25] Priya: Yes, keep long-lived connections where possible, use HTTP/2 multiplexing, and prefer internal load balancers or gRPC with keepalives to reduce ephemeral ports.
[06:35] Sara: Anything else about model serving runtime knobs — like KV cache TTLs, shard sizes, and garbage collection?
[06:41] Miguel: You can tune KV TTL to keep context for longer sessions but that uses memory. Shard sizes affect local cache hit rates: smaller shards more evenly distributed but more cross-node misses; larger shards increase locality but risk imbalance. We recommend starting with medium shard counts and observing hit-rate metrics via our Console. GC is mostly automatic but you can configure eviction thresholds.
[07:01] Evan: About benchmarks — will Redwood run a synthetic workload that mimics our traffic (mix of short chat and long generation)?
[07:07] Priya: Yes, we'll produce a perf script matching your mixes and run it in a customer-like network topology. We'll include measurements for p50/p90/p95 token latency, end-to-end request latency, and cost per 1M tokens.
[07:18] Sara: Please include cold start numbers and model reload times. Those are key for our SLA calculations.
[07:22] Miguel: Will do.
[07:24] Alex: Quick recap and next steps: Redwood to send network diagram/Terraform, perf plan and synthetic tests, security docs (SOC2, KMS, audits), and pricing/pilot contract. Customer to share VPC details and preferred timeline.
[07:36] Sara: Timeline: we'd like pilot in 4 weeks if network design is approved.
[07:40] Alex: Sounds good. Thanks all. We'll follow up with links.
[07:44] [END]
